newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: U.S. push on immigrant smuggling called success.
newsitem.headline: U.S. push on immigrant smuggling called success.

text.p: The number of Dominicans attempting the dangerous and illegal sea voyage to Puerto Rico has dropped sharply since the U.S. Coast Guard increased patrols of the waters surrounding the U.S. territory, a Coast Guard spokesman said on Thursday.

This month, the Coast Guard has intercepted only one boat with 64 Dominicans on board. He said 163 were picked up in January, 277 in November and 89 in October, the first month of the stepped-up patrols, part of an inter-agency operation known as "Frontier Shield."

"It looks like we have stopped the flow by as much as 50 percent," Coast Guard Capt. Thomas Bernard, commander of the Coast Guard's Greater Antilles Section, said in an interview at the San Juan Coast Guard base this week.

Since 1994, would-be illegal immigrants from the Dominican Republic have replaced Haitians and Cubans as the chief concern of Coast Guard crews patrolling the northern Caribbean Sea and Atlantic Ocean south of Florida.

The U.S. Immigration & Naturalisation Service estimates that some 20,000 Dominicans per year illegally reach Puerto Rico, many crammed onto small boats that make their way across the Mona Passage, the 100-mile (161-km) wide stretch of ocean that separates Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic.

While mass boatlifts of Haitians and Cubans, most recently in 1994, have attracted more attention, over time far more Dominicans have reached the United States, many of them heading for New York after reaching Puerto Rico.
"If you take any 10-year period of time, more Dominicans have entered the country illegally. But it almost goes unnoticed," Bernard said.

Bernard said it was impossible to tell how many died attempting the crossing. But he said that with the crowding on the boats and the notorious unpredictability of Mona Passage weather, it was inevitable that many had perished.
"Not very many of the Dominicans swim," he said.
Dominican authorities on Jan. 18 said some 18 people were missing and feared dead in a shipwreck off their coast tied to immigrant smuggling.
Coast Guard ships are in the Mona Passage every day and U.S. aircraft fly overhead, watching for the wooden "yolas" attempting the 22- to 24-hour journey.

Since the added patrols, immigrants have reported the price smugglers demand for the journey has gone up by about 20 percent to the equivalent of about $500. They also no longer promise "guaranteed" passage, in which they attempted the crossing repeatedy until they were successful.

In addition to the drop in interceptions, Bernard said Puerto Rico's west coast was no longer dotted with the abandoned boats, their engines gone, which were the tell-tale sign of a successful crossing.
